extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, applicants, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance from the USPTO on evaluating inventorship for AI-assisted inventions and on applying subject-matter-eligibility (SME) analysis to AI-related claims, plus rules and recommended practices for practitioners using AI tools in practice before the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor must be a natural person (35 U.S.C. 100(f))
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor must be a natural person; AI systems and other non-natural persons cannot be named as inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based on Thaler v. Vidal and USPTO interpretation of 35 U.S.C. 100(f): 'the individual or, if a joint invention, the individuals collectively who invented or discovered the subject matter of the invention.' The Office will not list non-natural persons as inventors even if AI was instrumental.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI-assisted inventions not categorically unpatentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an AI system (or other advanced tools) by a natural person does not preclude that person from qualifying as an inventor if they significantly contributed to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent applications and patents for AI-assisted inventions must name the natural person(s) who significantly contributed (meeting the Pannu factors). The guidance applies to utility, plant, and design patents and does not categorically render AI-assisted inventions unpatentable for inventorship reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pannu factors — three-part significant-contribution test
rubrics_metrics.description: Each named inventor must satisfy the three Pannu factors: (1) contribute in some significant manner to the conception or reduction to practice of the invention; (2) make a contribution that is not insignificant in quality relative to the full invention; (3) do more than merely explain well-known concepts or the state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to meet any one factor precludes being named inventor. The focus is on natural person contributions. Joint inventors can apply even if they made different types or amounts of contribution; contribution to a single claim is sufficient for a joint inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-by-claim, case-by-case application and per-claim natural-person requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Application of the Pannu factors is performed on a claim-by-claim and case-by-case basis; each claim must have at least one natural person inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a single person uses an AI system to create an invention, that person must make a significant contribution to every claim. No requirement that every named joint inventor contribute to every claim, but each claim must have at least one natural person inventor. If inventorship of a claim cannot be corrected because no natural person significantly contributed, the claim must be canceled or amended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp1 — AI use does not negate natural person's contributions
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural person’s use of an AI system in creating an AI-assisted invention does not negate the person’s contributions as an inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence or use of AI alone is not a reason to withhold inventorship from a qualifying natural person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp2 — mere problem recognition or general plan is not conception
rubrics_metrics.description: Merely recognizing a problem or having a general goal or research plan to pursue does not rise to the level of conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conception requires more than stating a desired result or plan; it requires a specific, definite idea of the invention's structure or operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp3 — reduction to practice alone insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing an invention to practice alone is not a significant contribution that rises to the level of inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work that only reduces to practice but does not contribute to conception or the substantive inventive aspects may not qualify as inventorship under Pannu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp4 — contribution via essential building blocks
rubrics_metrics.description: A natural person who develops an essential building block from which the claimed invention is derived may be considered to have provided a significant contribution even if they were not present for or a participant in each activity that led to conception of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing key enabling technology or components that are essential to the claimed invention can meet the significant-contribution standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guiding Principle Gp5 — intellectual domination of AI not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintaining 'intellectual domination' over an AI system does not, on its own, make a person an inventor of any inventions created through the use of the AI system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supervising, directing, or controlling an AI tool without making a qualifying inventive contribution does not satisfy inventorship requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship examples as analytic aides
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO issued two illustrative examples (transaxle for remote-control car and developing a therapeutic compound) to assist application of the inventorship guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are available on the USPTO AI resources page and illustrate how to apply the Pannu factors in concrete fact patterns; examples are illustrative and fact-specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments from AI systems should not be recorded
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignments from AI systems should not be recorded with the USPTO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ASP: only natural persons/entities appropriate under ownership rules should be recorded; non-natural person assignments are not acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose and duty of reasonable inquiry (37 CFR and ethics rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties identified in 37 CFR §§ 1.56(c), 1.555(a), and 42.11(a) owe a duty to disclose information material to patentability; 37 CFR 11.18(b) imposes a duty of reasonable inquiry and certification for those presenting papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certification that an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances was performed may include questions about whether and how AI was used in creating the invention. The duty to disclose is ongoing during prosecution (e.g., if claim amendments change inventorship issues).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner authority under 37 CFR §1.105 to request information
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may request information under 37 CFR §1.105; the requested information need not be material to patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requests may be made when there is a reasonable basis to conclude a party has information reasonably necessary to examination. Triggers include unclear inventorship suggesting no human significant contribution, contradictory applicant statements, or facts supporting a prima facie case that the named inventor(s) did not significantly contribute. Where appropriate, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. §§101 and 115 is permissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority/benefit claim requirements when foreign application names non-natural persons
rubrics_metrics.description: For a U.S. application claiming priority to a foreign application that names both natural and non-natural persons as joint inventors, the U.S. application data sheet must list only the natural person(s) who significantly contributed, and one of those natural persons must be common with the foreign application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures consistency of inventor listing across priority filings and avoids listing non-natural persons in the U.S. record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction of inventorship and claim amendment/cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: If contributions by a named inventor do not rise to inventorship, inventorship must be corrected; if inventorship of a claim cannot be corrected because no natural person significantly contributed, the claim must be canceled or amended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correction is required to maintain proper inventorship; inability to identify a qualifying natural person for a claim requires removing that claim from the patentable set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of AI-based tools by practitioners — permitted but governed by existing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of AI-based tools by practitioners and parties is not prohibited, but practitioners must follow existing rules and be aware of risks (accuracy, confidentiality, ethics). The guidance does not introduce new rules or duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice educates about risks and emphasizes that existing USPTO rules and professional conduct obligations apply to AI-assisted practice to mitigate risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document drafting and certification (37 CFR 11.18(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Individuals signing/presenting papers must comply with 37 CFR 11.18(b): certify and exercise a duty of reasonable inquiry; all associated individuals owe a duty of candor and good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No obligation to disclose use of specific AI tools unless specifically requested by the USPTO, but signers must ensure the veracity and reasonableness of filings prepared with AI assistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing/signature and account rules — AI cannot act as filing user
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers and filings must be signed by the submitting person; an AI tool cannot sign for a natural person. USPTO.gov accounts are limited to natural persons; practitioners may not sponsor AI tools as support staff to obtain accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure only authorized natural persons sign and use USPTO electronic filing; do not create accounts for or attribute agency to non-natural persons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interacting with USPTO IT and data-mining rules
rubrics_metrics.description: An AI system is not considered a 'user' for filing or accessing documents via USPTO electronic filing systems; use of tools for data mining USPTO databases is subject to the USPTO Terms of Use and permitted bulk data product terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unauthorized access or misuse of USPTO systems for AI tool operation may violate the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Use permitted bulk data products for appropriate data mining.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality, national security, and data-risk mitigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Using AI systems for searching or drafting can risk inadvertent disclosure of client-sensitive information, implicate national security/export-control/foreign-filing license issues, and risk data breaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should comply with Rules of Professional Conduct, understand AI tools' terms of use, privacy policies, and cybersecurity practices, and take steps to mitigate confidentiality and security risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME Step 2A Prong One — identifying claims that recite abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong One evaluates whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception (abstract idea), including mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2024 update provides additional discussion on claims that do not recite abstract ideas and on those that do, informed by recent case law and USPTO-issued examples. Determination relies on claim language and how it maps to abstract-idea groupings.

rubrics_metrics.name: SME Step 2A Prong Two — improvements analysis for AI inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A Prong Two examines whether limitations integrate an abstract idea into a practical application (e.g., provide an improvement to the functioning of a computer or another technology) or otherwise supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For AI inventions, specific steps showing how the output of an AI (e.g., using ANN output to solve a technological problem) amount to an improvement to computer functioning or a technical field can render the claim eligible. Distinguish improvements to the abstract idea vs improvements to computer/technical functioning. Particular treatment/prophylaxis limitations can render claims eligible; generic treatment steps may not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example-based eligibility teaching points (Examples 47–49)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypothetical examples illustrate SME analysis for AI inventions: Example 47 (anomaly detection) shows using ANN output to remediate network attacks in real time constitutes an improvement; Example 48 (speech separation) shows specific speech-separation techniques can improve technological functioning; Example 49 (fibrosis treatment) shows particular treatment steps and applying a weighted PRS model and ML model in a personalized medicine context can render claims eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are illustrative and fact-specific; a claim need not mirror an example to be eligible. Training and examiner guidance accompany the examples. Key teaching points: specific technical improvements, particular treatment steps, and explicit recitation of how AI outputs are used to improve technology or practice support eligibility.
